headline: High risk of shared-workspace data leakage and capability conflict; prompt-injection and cascading-error risks are moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents read and write project-local files by default, and agent_a explicitly uses a per-project shared directory while agent_b runs local development workflows. That creates a plausible file-based instruction bridge even without MCP or clipboard. The interaction is inferred from docs, not directly observed, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF agent_b ingests files from the shared project directory as instructions, injected content can steer its outputs.
IF agent_a writes attacker-controlled text into files that agent_b later parses, prompt injection becomes feasible.
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct directories.
Disable automatic file ingestion for agent_b.
Review any generated markdown or prompt files before reuse.
Use a read-only handoff file for inter-agent communication.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for shared files.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have filesystem read/write access and touch sensitive classes: agent_a handles generated source code and agent_b handles configuration secrets plus paper data. A shared project or local development workspace can expose files across the pair. Because the profiles document local file access but not direct cross-agent isolation, the leakage pathway is plausible and medium severity.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same project directory, files written by one are readable by the other.
IF agent_b loads .env or notebook files from the shared workspace, configuration secrets may be exposed.
mitigations: Move secrets to a separate directory outside the shared workspace.
Restrict file permissions on .env and notebook artifacts.
Run each agent in a different working directory.
Delete transient outputs after each run.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem sandboxing.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shells, install packages, and write files, so they can contend for the same mutable workspace. Neither profile states locking or coordination primitives, and agent_a explicitly shares state via the project directory. This is a default-capable overlap, but not enough evidence for high because git mutation is false in both profiles.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory concurrently, file clobbering can occur.
IF package installation happens in the same environment, dependency drift can break one agent's run.
mitigations: Serialize writes to the shared directory.
Use separate virtual environments.
Pin dependencies before running either agent.
Snapshot the workspace before each run.
requires-engineering: add file locks around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent_a is a coding agent that writes files then offers to run code, while agent_b is a content-writing/RAG agent with API endpoints for ask and agentic-ask. If agent_b consumes agent_a's generated code or text as authoritative, errors can propagate into downstream outputs. The profiles suggest the pathway but do not prove direct automation, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a's generated files as source material without verification, mistakes cascade into its outputs.
IF agent_a's generated code is executed and its results are reused by agent_b, errors can amplify.
mitigations: Require human review before reuse of generated artifacts.
Add a verification step before agent_b consumes agent_a outputs.
Keep generated code and narrative outputs in separate folders.
Log provenance for reused artifacts.
requires-engineering: implement automated validation gates.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent_b explicitly handles configuration secrets and runs local development workflows, while agent_a also handles OPENAI_API_KEY and executes generated code with user privileges. The pair therefore concentrates sensitive material in environments with different operational assumptions, creating a compliance and retention mismatch risk. No direct residency breach is documented, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF either agent logs secrets or notebook outputs persist, retention policy violations can occur.
IF sensitive data is moved between the local development environment and the coding workspace, compliance scope expands.
mitigations: Mask secrets in logs immediately.
Purge notebook outputs before sharing artifacts.
Store secrets in a dedicated secret manager.
Document retention rules for both environments.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls across both stacks.
